title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms
authors: Yifeng Peng, Bin Yan, Harshal Shah, Srinivasan Raghuraman, Kim Wagner, Sunpreet Singh Arora
abstract: Repeated measurements are a major bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We uncover and characterize parameter-specific sparsity in the matrix of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients: most absolute contribution mass concentrates in a subset of groups whose relevance varies across parameters and optimization states. Building on this structure, we introduce a learned controller that predicts group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, then selects measurements through a tunable coverage threshold. Exact contributions provide offline supervision without being required at deployment. Across 15 molecular VQE settings, our method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC. We then ask whether large language models (LLMs) can solve the same selection problem without fine-tuning. The results reveal both promise and a clear limitation: LLMs can identify useful measurement groups, yet without guidance, local models do not consistently prioritize the physical information that matters most. Our learned controller uses these cues more effectively. This contrast points toward a broader direction for AI-assisted science: combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.

infographic.key_insight: Parameter-specific sparsity lets a learned controller measure only the qubit-wise commuting groups most relevant to variational quantum gradients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Selective measurement can reduce VQE shot requirements while retaining energy accuracy close to measuring all QWC groups.
method: Characterize how gradient-contribution relevance varies across parameters and optimization states.
Predict group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features.
Select measurements using a tunable coverage threshold, with exact contributions needed only for offline supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15 molecular VQE settings, the method saved 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa relative to Full-QWC.
infographic.watch_item: The reported savings concern nominal measurement shots; end-to-end runtime benefits and generalization beyond the evaluated settings remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms

title: Restoring quantum neural network trainability through reusable calibration
authors: Ruizhe Shen, Xianquan Yan, Kenji Kawaguchi, Ching Hua Lee
abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) rely on measured quantum observables to guide optimization, but hardware noise can suppress the parameter-dependent signals essential for learning. Here, we develop a structure-preserving error-mitigation framework that improves QNN trainability through reusable calibration of the quantum circuit's effective noise response. By calibrating a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit, we construct regularized estimators of local quantum features that remain fixed throughout training. We quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect the recovery of both observables and their derivatives. Numerical simulations demonstrate enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and improved classification performance, and an IBM Quantum experiment confirms improved closed-loop variational optimization under hardware noise. We further demonstrate calibration reuse in a modular QNN comprising 25 independent four-qubit channels, corresponding to 100 qubits in aggregate. Our results establish reusable feature calibration as a practical approach to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without repeated calibration at every training step.

infographic.key_insight: Reusable, architecture-matched calibration can recover noise-suppressed quantum features and improve quantum neural network trainability without recalibrating at every training step.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fixed feature estimators offer a practical way to improve noise-limited quantum learning while avoiding repeated calibration during optimization.
method: Calibrate a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit.
Construct regularized estimators of local quantum features and keep them fixed throughout training.
Quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect recovered observables and derivatives.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations showed improved landscape contrast, convergence, and classification; an IBM Quantum experiment improved closed-loop optimization, and a modular demonstration reused calibration across 25 independent four-qubit channels.
infographic.watch_item: Calibration accuracy and noise-response matching remain critical; the 100-qubit aggregate demonstration comprises independent four-qubit channels, not one fully coupled 100-qubit QNN.
infographic.paper_title: Restoring quantum neural network trainability through reusable calibration

title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
authors: Yueen Chen, Mohammad Sharifian, Abolfazl Bayat
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

infographic.key_insight: Ensembling variational quantum regressors improves nonlinear function prediction, with sequential AdaBoost achieving significantly better accuracy than independently trained Bagging.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a way to combine imperfect quantum regressors for nonlinear modeling without requiring fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
method: Train variational quantum regressors independently with Bagging or sequentially with AdaBoost.
Select features from first- and second-order polynomial terms.
Use repeated feature encoding to map features to qubits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on four benchmark functions with varying nonlinearity reports improved performance as ensemble size and individual regressor size increase.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish practical quantum advantage or quantify robustness on noisy quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning

title: Variational Corrections to Strong-Disorder Renormalization in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Field Ising Model on Quantum Hardware
authors: Alina Joch, Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract: Strong-disorder renormalization-group (SDRG) methods provide an effective description of disordered quantum many-body systems by identifying the dominant couplings for the low energy physics. However, the resulting renormalization-group flow is approximate and neglects correlations beyond the RG description. Here, we investigate whether variational quantum optimization can be used to correct these approximations. Building on the emergent-coupling-based ansatz (ECBA) developed for the one-dimensional random Heisenberg model, we introduce a formulation adapted to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model. The SDRG flow determines the structure of the circuit, while variational optimization allows the state to deviate from the RG approximation. We study the resulting ansatz numerically and experimentally on an IQM superconducting quantum processor. For a 16-qubit system, we perform full variational optimization on the quantum processor, while a 49-qubit system is investigated using pre-optimized parameters, achieving a relative energy accuracy of 89% and 97%, respectively. Our results demonstrate that RG information can be translated into shallow, hardware-compatible quantum circuits while variational optimization enables corrections beyond the underlying RG approximation also for two-dimensional systems.

infographic.key_insight: An SDRG-guided variational circuit corrects renormalization approximations for the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model on quantum hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Renormalization-group structure provides a route to shallow, hardware-compatible circuits for disordered quantum many-body simulations.
method: Adapt the emergent-coupling-based ansatz to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model.
Use the SDRG flow to determine quantum circuit structure.
Optimize circuit parameters to capture correlations beyond the SDRG approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical and IQM superconducting-processor evaluations report relative energy accuracies of 89% for 16 qubits with full hardware optimization and 97% for 49 qubits using pre-optimized parameters.
infographic.watch_item: The 49-qubit result uses pre-optimized parameters, so full variational optimization on hardware at that scale remains un demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Corrections to Strong-Disorder Renormalization in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Field Ising Model on Quantum Hardware

title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
authors: Davi Castro-Silva, Ryan Dancy, Sergii Strelchuk
abstract: Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Some classically polynomial-time graph properties cannot be computed by polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width o(n/log n), even at unrestricted depth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For symmetry-preserving quantum designs, circuit size alone is insufficient: limited entanglement width can prevent efficient computation of otherwise tractable graph properties.
method: Define entanglement width by the largest necessary state-factor block across layers and computational-basis inputs.
Use a partial-trace-based quantum pebble game to transfer classical indistinguishability lower bounds.
Construct polynomial-size symmetric circuits for BQP graph properties without entanglement restrictions and an efficient symmetric QAOA implementation for MAX 3XOR.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports formal lower bounds and constructive expressivity results, not empirical benchmarks or hardware evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The lower bound applies to symmetry-constrained circuit families and does not establish an entanglement requirement for unrestricted quantum algorithms.
infographic.paper_title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits

title: Generative Models using Multi-layer Quantum Extreme Learning Machines
authors: Amir Azzam, M. Pilar Casado, Michele Grossi, Arnau Riera, Sofia Vallecorsa
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) and the closely related quantum extreme learning machine (QELM) paradigm exploit the complex dynamics of an uncontrolled quantum system for machine learning, offering an alternative to variational quantum algorithms whose training is hindered by barren plateaus and costly circuit optimization. Because the quantum system itself is left fixed, learning reduces to fitting a linear readout of a set of measured observables, and no gradient is ever taken through the quantum device. In this work we repurpose this paradigm for generative modeling: a fixed, randomly initialized multi-layer QELM transforms a scalar latent variable into a rich vector of measured expectation values, and only a simple linear readout is trained to map these to samples of a target distribution. The readout is fitted by minimizing the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target samples. We show that this algorithm is capable of reproducing a range of one- and two-dimensional distributions. Moreover, encoding the class label on dedicated qubits enables conditional generation of different classes of distributions with the same linear readout. We show that this cannot be achieved by the linear readout alone, and that the reservoir dynamics play a role in the ability to distinguish the different classes of distributions. We also show that using a simple six-qubit reservoir one is able to generate handwritten digits from the Digits and MNIST datasets with high accuracy. Moreover, replacing the Haar-random dynamics by time evolution under several physical Hamiltonians leaves the performance unchanged, provided the evolution spreads the input across the register. Finally, we show that a classical random Fourier feature model of the same size performs equally well: at the sizes we study, the QELM offers no advantage over its classical counterpart.

infographic.key_insight: A fixed multi-layer quantum extreme learning machine can generate target distributions by training only a linear readout, but matches rather than outperforms a same-size classical random Fourier feature model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Keeping the quantum reservoir fixed eliminates quantum-circuit optimization and gradients through the device, simplifying training while retaining measurement costs.
method: Map a scalar latent variable to measured expectation values using a fixed, randomly initialized quantum reservoir.
Train a linear readout by minimizing maximum mean discrepancy between generated and target samples.
Encode class labels on dedicated qubits for conditional generation with a shared readout.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study demonstrates one- and two-dimensional distribution generation and handwritten-digit generation from Digits and MNIST using a six-qubit reservoir; physical Hamiltonian dynamics preserve performance when inputs spread across the register.
infographic.watch_item: No quantum advantage is demonstrated at the studied sizes, and performance depends on reservoir dynamics spreading the encoded input.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Models using Multi-layer Quantum Extreme Learning Machines

title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
authors: Luca Hofele, Yongxin Song, Áron Márton, Ian Hesner, Ilya Besedin, Jakob Ekert
abstract: Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

infographic.key_insight: Lattice surgery enabled logical-state teleportation between two distance-three surface-code qubits on a 41-physical-qubit superconducting circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results inform gate-sequence and timing choices for implementing operations between logical qubits in fault-tolerant quantum processors.
method: Merge two surface-code patches using lattice surgery.
Track logical observables to characterize information transfer from source to target.
Repeat stabilizer measurements and optimize gate count and sequence duration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The experiment found that repeated post-merge stabilizer measurements restored fault tolerance and increased teleportation fidelity, with further gains from protocol optimization.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstration uses distance-three codes; the abstract provides no numerical fidelities or evidence of scaling to larger logical circuits.
infographic.paper_title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
authors: Hansol Noh, Unam Oh, Sangkyu Baek, Doyeol, Ahn
abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

infographic.key_insight: Combining polynomial reduced-order models with quantum transport preserves nonlinear flow dynamics while making per-step rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with grid cells per coordinate at fixed model dimension and drift degree.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reduced-model polynomial degree becomes a design variable for balancing flow-model accuracy against early fault-tolerant quantum hardware costs.
method: Fit polynomial reduced-order models using sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics.
Implement Koopman–von Neumann transport with Walsh-synthesized quantum circuits.
Estimate end-to-end costs using surface-code resource models.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, the study estimates 1.62 hours on about 560,000 physical qubits for 1% relative RMS field error against the radial model, and demonstrates nonlinear radial transport on IBM hardware with reference-circuit noise mitigation.
infographic.watch_item: The fault-tolerant runtimes are estimates, with three-coordinate wake cases spanning hours to weeks; the reported 1% error is measured against a reduced radial model.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime

title: Rate-1/2 Quantum LDPC Codes for Multi-tier Superconducting Hardware
authors: Jiaxuan Zhang, Zhao-Yun Chen, Jia-Ning Li, Tian-Hao Wei, Qing-Yang Hou, Wei-Cheng Kong
abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for scalable quantum computing, while its resource overhead is governed in large part by the encoding rate, namely the number of logical qubits encoded per physical data qubit. Recent quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) constructions have entered the ultra-high-rate regime with encoding rates above 1/2, but their syndrome-extraction circuits generally rely on reconfigurable connectivity or long-range qubit transport, making them difficult to implement on fixed-connectivity superconducting hardware. Here we introduce Armillary codes, a family of ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes whose algebraic structure is generated by native iSWAP routing under hardware constraints. The construction jointly enforces stabilizer commutation and correct parallel syndrome extraction, while admitting radial and circumferential couplings in crossing-free routing layers. We construct explicit codes with rates above 1/2, stabilizer weight 12, Tanner-graph girth 6, and distances from 12 to 16, with layouts on 5 or 6 hardware tiers. Compared with the Gross and Mitten codes at the same distances, the Armillary codes achieve encoding rates about 6 and 2.5 times those of the Gross and Mitten codes, respectively, while maintaining lower hardware-complexity scores. In circuit-level simulations, the \([\![8688,4348,16]\!]\) code approaches the teraquop regime, achieving a logical error rate of \(1.62\times10^{-12}\) per logical qubit per round at a physical error rate of 0.1\%. These results show that the rate-\(1/2\) regime of qLDPC codes can be extended from reconfigurable platforms to superconducting hardware, providing a route toward low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum processors.

infographic.key_insight: Armillary qLDPC codes encode more than one logical qubit per two data qubits while supporting fixed-connectivity superconducting hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: High encoding rates and crossing-free routing layers offer a path to lower-overhead fault-tolerant superconducting processors.
method: Generate code structure from native iSWAP routing under hardware constraints.
Jointly enforce stabilizer commutation and correct parallel syndrome extraction.
Use radial and circumferential couplings across 5–6 hardware tiers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Circuit-level simulations of the [[8688,4348,16]] code yield a logical error rate of 1.62×10⁻¹² per logical qubit per round at 0.1% physical error; constructed codes have distances of 12–16.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based; realizing 5–6 hardware tiers and weight-12 stabilizer measurements remains an implementation challenge.
infographic.paper_title: Rate-1/2 Quantum LDPC Codes for Multi-tier Superconducting Hardware

title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
authors: Bolin Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Yongguang Lv, Ruiqing He, Hengliang Guo, Jiandong Shang
abstract: Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50\%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21\% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01\% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.

infographic.key_insight: SCOPE compiles quantum circuits for shorter physical execution time using an operator Schmidt time surrogate rather than gate count or circuit depth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Latency-guided compilation can help engineers shorten pulse schedules on coherence-limited quantum devices while avoiding pulse optimization for every structural candidate.
method: Estimate nonlocal implementation time from distance to product operators and a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound.
Combine this estimate with trace-angle and waveform constraints to guide genetic-search fitness and mutation-region selection.
Use local quantum optimal control (QOC) to determine final pulse durations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances beat adapted EPOC, with a 42.50% equally weighted reduction in eight-run mean QOC critical-path duration and a 2.00× geometric mean speedup.
infographic.watch_item: Results are numerical and control-model-specific; performance on physical hardware and other device constraints remains to be validated.
infographic.paper_title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework

title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry
authors: Qianjun Yao, Jie Liu, He Li
abstract: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

infographic.key_insight: Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) recovers correlation lost during stabilizer projection, improving quantum chemistry accuracy without enlarging the retained quantum register.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SSPT can help resource-constrained quantum chemistry workflows reach chemical precision with fewer contextual qubits.
method: Use Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection to generate external states from an optimized CS-VQE reference.
Estimate energy corrections with Epstein–Nesbet-type second-order perturbation theory or an external-space resolvent.
Evaluate required matrix elements through reduced-register Pauli expectation values, avoiding full-space wave-function reconstruction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Molecular benchmarks report substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors and chemical precision with fewer contextual qubits in several cases; the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify measurement overhead or external-space scaling, leaving the total resource trade-off uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry

title: Quantum Information Transfer in Molecular Polaritonic Networks: A Van Vleck Effective-Hamiltonian Approach
authors: Saad Yalouz, Vincent Pouthier
abstract: Achieving high-fidelity transfer of an arbitrary quantum state between spatially separated qubits is a central challenge for reliable quantum hardware. We address this question within a polaritonic framework by introducing Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT). Based on quasidegenerate perturbation theory, this approach describes a molecular network coupled to an optical cavity and local phonons through a generalized Holstein--Tavis--Cummings Hamiltonian. Quantum information is encoded in a coherent superposition of exciton-cavity states, while phonons constitute a weakly coupled environment. In the nonadiabatic regime of weak exciton-phonon coupling, the method incorporates phonon-induced renormalization of polaritonic states and their dynamics while reducing the Hamiltonian to independent fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron-polariton subblocks. This structure provides efficient access to the coherence and population propagators governing quantum-state transfer without invoking a Markovian approximation. We benchmark the approach against exact dynamics for a molecular wheel network, considering both molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer. PB-VVPT accurately reproduces short- and long-time transfer dynamics, including thermal decoherence and fidelity revivals consistent with non-Markovian memory effects, with prediction errors below $1\%$ over most of the simulated time intervals. This accuracy is achieved with an estimated diagonalization cost more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of the exact reference calculations. These results establish PB-VVPT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach to quantum information transfer in molecular polaritonic networks.

infographic.key_insight: Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT) efficiently predicts quantum-state transfer in molecular polaritonic networks while retaining phonon-driven decoherence and memory effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support computationally efficient design and evaluation of cavity-coupled molecular networks for quantum information transfer.
method: Model molecules, an optical cavity, and local phonons with a generalized Holstein–Tavis–Cummings Hamiltonian.
Use quasidegenerate perturbation theory to construct fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron–polariton subblocks.
Compute coherence and population propagators without a Markovian approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against exact molecular-wheel dynamics, PB-VVPT reproduced molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer with errors below 1% over most simulated intervals and an estimated diagonalization cost over 100× lower.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to simulated molecular-wheel networks in the nonadiabatic, weak exciton–phonon coupling regime; broader applicability remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Information Transfer in Molecular Polaritonic Networks: A Van Vleck Effective-Hamiltonian Approach

title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction
authors: Alec Eickbusch, Nick Noll, Michael Newman, Matt McEwen, Leigh S. Martin, Alexis Morvan
abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.

infographic.key_insight: Temporally correlated leakage limits quantum error correction, but a walking stability circuit suppresses it and lowers the logical error floor by two orders of magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Suppressing higher-state leakage and adapting syndrome-extraction duration could improve the reliability and time efficiency of fault-tolerant quantum processors.
method: Scale surface-code stability experiments from 3×3 to 7×7 patches on a 105-qubit Willow processor.
Model heating to |3⟩ and higher-state transport with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model.
Implement a walking stability circuit and evaluate decoder-confidence-based adaptive termination offline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments achieved temporal block suppression μ_T = 1.47 ± 0.25 and a walking-circuit logical error floor ≤3.20×10⁻⁸ at 60 cycles; offline adaptive termination reduced spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% versus the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.
infographic.watch_item: Ionizing-radiation bursts limit the remaining error floor, and adaptive termination was evaluated offline rather than demonstrated in real-time control.
infographic.paper_title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction

title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
authors: José Daniel Viqueira, Andrés Gómez, David Mera
abstract: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

infographic.key_insight: Variational quantum recurrent neural networks match classical baselines overall, with one variant showing higher average capacity on a joint memory–nonlinearity task.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Task-driven capacity benchmarking helps engineers compare recurrent architectures before deploying them for time series prediction.
method: Quantify memory and nonlinear processing capacity using task-driven benchmarks.
Compare variational quantum recurrent networks with classical recurrent baselines.
Assess how model size and parameter initialization affect performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses two generic benchmark tasks and a synthetic chaotic-system dataset; classical models scale better with memory size over the studied range.
infographic.watch_item: Larger quantum models become more sensitive to initialization, reducing the probability of finding good solutions.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction

title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring
authors: Soumyadip Sahoo, Sahinur Reja
abstract: Increasing circuit depth is expected to improve a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We show that this expectation can fail, and that curing the failure does not guarantee the exact ground state. We study a symmetry-preserving ansatz of SingleExcitationMinus gates, started from the Néel state, on the frustrated spin-$1/2$ $J_1$--$J_2$ Heisenberg ring with $N=10$ and $12$ sites. With random initialization the fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin change abruptly at intermediate depth ($L\approx 9$ for $N=10$, $L=10$--$12$ for $N=12$), giving improvement, degradation and recovery, a double-descent-like shape. The circuit family is nested and the gradient stays finite, so this is an optimization failure, not a loss of expressibility or a barren plateau. A chained warm start, which extends an optimized shallow circuit with identity layers, removes the collapse and improves energy error and fidelity almost monotonically for most frustration values. However, near $J_2/J_1=0.60$ ($N=10$) and over $J_2/J_1=0.60$--$1.00$ ($N=12$) the warm start stalls at a fidelity of $\approx 0.50$--$0.58$, although the energy error is small and the total spin stays in the $S=0$ sector. Removing the non-monotonic depth dependence is therefore not the same as reaching the ground state, and low energy and a singlet-like state are not sufficient: the fidelity, entropy and total spin must be satisfied together. The conclusions are limited to the system sizes and frustration values studied.

infographic.key_insight: Deeper symmetry-preserving VQE circuits can suffer an optimization collapse, while warm starts remove that collapse without guaranteeing the exact ground state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Initialize deeper circuits from optimized shallower ones, and assess fidelity, entropy and total spin together rather than relying on low energy alone.
method: Study 10- and 12-site frustrated J1–J2 Heisenberg rings using SingleExcitationMinus circuits initialized in the Néel state.
Compare random initialization with chained warm starts that append identity layers to optimized circuits.
Track fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin across circuit depths.
infographic.evidence_signal: Random initialization shows collapse near depth 9 for 10 sites and depths 10–12 for 12 sites; warm starts largely restore monotonic improvement but stall at fidelity ≈0.50–0.58 near J2/J1=0.60 for 10 sites and across 0.60–1.00 for 12 sites.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the studied sizes and frustration values; finite gradients and nested circuits identify the observed collapse as optimization failure, not a barren plateau or lost expressibility.
infographic.paper_title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring

title: Double-Bracket Quantum Algorithms for Preparing Multiple Excited States
authors: Salahuddin Abdul Rahman, Özkan Karabacak, Rafal Wisniewski
abstract: Many problems in quantum chemistry, many-body physics, and optimization require excited states of a Hamiltonian. Double-bracket quantum algorithms compile circuits recursively from evolutions under the Hamiltonian and a second operator, without a parameterized ansatz. They have been proposed for several tasks, such as diagonalization and the preparation of ground and thermal states. In this work, we extend this framework to excited states. Combining the ensemble approach with double-bracket flows, we introduce the Double-Bracket quantum algorithm for Multiple EXcited states (DB-MEX), which evolves $p+1$ orthonormal states toward low-lying eigenstates of the Hamiltonian with a single recursively compiled quantum circuit, so they remain orthonormal by construction. The circuit approximates a double-bracket flow of a weighted sum of projectors onto the evolving states, whose number and weights are design parameters. The number of states sets the highest targeted excited state, and the weights determine whether the algorithm prepares the $p+1$ lowest eigenstates, only the $p$-th excited state, or only the span of the $p+1$ lowest eigenstates. In the latter case, a post-processing step recovers the individual eigenstates from their span. We show that the double-bracket flow and, for small step sizes, its discretization converge to the target for almost all initial states, with explicit local rates given by products of weight and energy gaps.

infographic.key_insight: DB-MEX uses one recursively compiled quantum circuit to evolve multiple orthonormal states toward selected low-energy eigenstates or their shared subspace.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers an ansatz-free route to excited-state preparation for quantum chemistry, many-body simulation, and Hamiltonian-based optimization.
method: Combine an ensemble of p+1 orthonormal states with a double-bracket flow of their weighted projectors.
Recursively compile a shared circuit from evolutions under the Hamiltonian and a second operator, preserving orthonormality.
Choose weights to target individual low-energy eigenstates, only the p-th excited state, or a low-energy subspace with post-processing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports convergence guarantees for almost all initial states, including small-step discretizations, with explicit local rates determined by products of weight and energy gaps.
infographic.watch_item: Practical circuit depth and noise tolerance are not established in the abstract, and discretized convergence requires sufficiently small steps.
infographic.paper_title: Double-Bracket Quantum Algorithms for Preparing Multiple Excited States

title: Proven optimality for LABS with quantum-classical branch and bound
authors: András Czégel
abstract: Low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) are the phase codes of pulse compression radar and the synchronization words of digital communication, and finding the sequence of a given length whose aperiodic autocorrelations have the smallest sum of squares is a hard binary optimization problem. The quantum optimization methods tested on LABS so far return good sequences, but they cannot show that a sequence is optimal or bound how far from optimal it may be. We show that a quantum optimization algorithm can deliver proven optimality. In our quantum-classical branch and bound, fixed-angle QAOA samples the Hamiltonians of the nodes of the search tree, its samples supply candidate sequences and the branching choice, and classical bounds prune the tree, so that the algorithm returns either a proof of optimality or, if it is stopped early, the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap. It works on the native quartic Hamiltonian without penalty terms, and its correctness does not depend on the sampler. With QAOA at depth p= 12 and at p= 1 and 1,000 shots per node, it proved the optima of all lengths from 2 to 30, where from length 27 on the root node is split without being sampled. Every run records both bounds against time, and its primal-dual integral measures its convergence. We claim no speedup.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum-classical branch and bound can certify globally optimal low-autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS), with correctness independent of the quantum sampler.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Certified LABS optimization supports the design of pulse-compression radar phase codes and digital-communication synchronization words.
method: Use fixed-angle QAOA on native quartic node Hamiltonians without penalty terms.
Use quantum samples to propose candidate sequences and guide branching; apply classical bounds to prune.
Return a proof of optimality or, if stopped early, the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported runs at QAOA depths p=12 and p=1 with 1,000 shots per sampled node proved optima for lengths 2–30; from length 27 onward, roots were split without sampling.
infographic.watch_item: No speedup is claimed, and the reported results do not establish scalability beyond length 30.
infographic.paper_title: Proven optimality for LABS with quantum-classical branch and bound

title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
authors: Xusheng Xu, Runqing Zhang, Hongtao Xue, Jize Han, Jingwei Wen, Ruoyu Zhou
abstract: quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.

infographic.key_insight: quspect selects routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis, reducing two-qubit gate counts compared with established compiler baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Jointly considering routing and resynthesis can produce shallower, lower-entangling-gate circuits for connectivity-constrained quantum hardware.
method: Screen routing candidates and compare their post-resynthesis costs.
Use parity-state A* for small CNOT-phase regions and heuristic synthesis for larger regions.
Apply numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 55 circuits from 41 papers on five topologies, quspect used 0.616× Qiskit O3's two-qubit gates (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval: 0.555–0.679) and 0.592× its depth; it also achieved the fewest CZ gates in all six main-run hardware scenarios.
infographic.watch_item: A* certifies minimum CX count only for a fixed phase polynomial when it reaches a goal within budget, not global optimality of the full compilation.
infographic.paper_title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis

title: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout
authors: Sadman Ahmed Shanto, Saikat Das, Eli M. Levenson-Falk
abstract: Electromagnetic simulations of device layouts to extract capacitance are computationally intensive, a major obstacle to accurate design of circuit devices. Machine learning models can bypass these simulations, but previous approaches have been restricted to layouts using only particular components, and require thousands of simulations of those same components as training data. We present QCap, a model that accurately predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of an arbitrary superconducting device layout in seconds, compared to minutes to hours of Ansys Q3D simulations. We develop a novel design-embedding algorithm that converts the layout into a universal graph format, allowing the model to work with any layout created with any tool. To achieve high accuracy, we obtain a coarse physics prior from a fast method of moments simulation of capacitance, then train the model to correct this prior. On 4,009 test designs withheld from training data the model outputs agree with Q3D simulations to a median error of 0.177%, and on never-seen component families it stays below 1% error. We demonstrate the model's scaling by obtaining the capacitance matrix of a 9-superconducting-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop (compared to 19.9 h and 228 GB of memory in Ansys) with sub-percent error, and capacitance of a (too large to simulate) 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 min on a laptop. We provide the open-source models and data on SQuADDS and Hugging Face. Our results provide a powerful tool for large-scale accurate circuit design and guide the development of models to bypass other physical simulations.

infographic.key_insight: QCap combines a graph neural network with a coarse physics prior to predict superconducting-device capacitance matrices rapidly and accurately.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast capacitance extraction can accelerate superconducting-circuit design, with a 9-qubit layout evaluated in 12 seconds on a laptop versus 19.9 hours in Ansys Q3D.
method: Embed planar device layouts into a universal graph representation.
Compute a coarse capacitance prior using a fast method-of-moments simulation.
Train a graph neural network to correct the physics prior.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against Q3D, QCap achieved 0.177% median error on 4,009 held-out designs and below 1% error on unseen component families; a 100-qubit, 781-conductor layout ran in 3.4 minutes on a laptop.
infographic.watch_item: The 100-qubit example was too large for reference simulation, so its runtime demonstrates scale but not independently verified accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout

title: Commutator-guided repair and classical-accessibility boundaries for shallow quantum circuits
authors: Yifeng Peng, Sunpreet Singh Arora, Harshal Shah, Srinivasan Raghuraman, Kim Wagner, Bin Yan
abstract: Trainability does not guarantee low-energy arrival: a shallow quantum circuit can be optimizable yet fail, under fixed depth and evaluation budgets, to reach Hamiltonian-selected states. We introduce a commutator-guided repair for this operational failure mode. Low-order host--Hamiltonian commutators and fixed same-support companion axes define a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations, from which a compact completion layer is selected before full reoptimization. Across 189 paired six-qubit trials, unrepaired circuits achieve 0/189 strict successes, a non-deployable per-trial control envelope achieves 109/189, and two predeclared selectors achieve 133/189 and 127/189. The repair loses to matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and remains size-limited for weighted MIS. Under fixed-depth geometric locality, repaired losses and gradients are classically computable, while corresponding ground-state targets admit low-bond-dimension tensor-network approximations through the tested sizes. The method reveals a trainability--arrival--classical-accessibility tradeoff rather than quantum advantage.

infographic.key_insight: Commutator-guided local circuit repair improves low-energy arrival in shallow quantum circuits, but does not establish quantum advantage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Under fixed depth and evaluation budgets, improving circuit trainability alone may not deliver the desired low-energy states.
method: Build a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations from low-order host–Hamiltonian commutators and fixed same-support companion axes.
Select a compact completion layer using predeclared selectors.
Fully reoptimize the repaired circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 189 paired six-qubit trials, unrepaired circuits had 0 strict successes, versus 109 for a non-deployable per-trial control envelope and 133 and 127 for two predeclared repair selectors.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits are problem- and size-dependent: repair loses to matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and remains size-limited for weighted MIS; classical accessibility also limits advantage claims.
infographic.paper_title: Commutator-guided repair and classical-accessibility boundaries for shallow quantum circuits
